raw_text:
### Introduction

Chronic heart failure (HF) remains a leading cause of global morbidity, mortality, and healthcare expenditure [1]. Despite major advances in guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT), including angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors, sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, a substantial portion of patients remain symptomatic [2]. For patients with a reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (HFrEF) and a prolonged QRS duration (especially left bundle branch block), cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) is highly effective [3]. However, nearly 70% of HFrEF patients present with a narrow QRS duration and are thus ineligible for CRT [4]. For this massive, medically refractory patient cohort, cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) has emerged as a promising device-based therapeutic option [5]. Delivering non-excitatory electrical signals directly to the myocardium, CCM bridges a critical therapeutic gap. This narrative review discusses the cellular mechanisms, clinical trial evidence, long-term safety, and future directions of CCM in contemporary heart failure care.

### Mechanisms of Action

Unlike conventional pacemakers or CRT devices that deliver electrical pulses to trigger myocardial depolarization and coordinate contraction, CCM delivers relatively high-voltage, long-duration biphasic signals during the absolute refractory period of the action potential [6]. Because these signals are non-excitatory, they do not trigger a new depolarization or alter the native cardiac rhythm. Instead, they modulate intracellular signaling pathways, improving both systolic and diastolic performance [7]. At the cellular level, CCM acutely enhances excitation-contraction coupling. In the failing heart, calcium cycling is severely impaired, characterized by depressed activity of the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase 2a (SERCA2a) and decreased phosphorylation of its regulatory protein, phospholamban (PLB). CCM therapy acutely restores PLB phosphorylation and upregulates SERCA2a activity, facilitating efficient calcium reuptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum during diastole and enhancing calcium release during systole [8].

Over intermediate and long terms, chronic delivery of CCM signals reverses the maladaptive "fetal gene program" toward a normal adult gene expression profile [9]. This molecular remodeling is not confined to the site of lead implantation in the right ventricular septum; over several months, the beneficial effects extend globally to remote regions of the left ventricle, promoting reverse structural remodeling [10]. Importantly, this improvement in contractile performance occurs without a concomitant increase in myocardial oxygen consumption, thereby optimizing overall myocardial mechano-energetic efficiency and coronary perfusion [11].

### Clinical Trial Evidence

The safety and clinical efficacy of CCM have been established through sequential prospective clinical trials. Initial safety and feasibility were confirmed in early pilot and cohort studies [12, 13]. The first randomized, double-blind, crossover trial, FIX-HF-4, demonstrated that three months of active CCM therapy significantly improved peak oxygen consumption (peak $\text{VO}_2$) and quality of life, measured by the Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire (MLHFQ), compared to sham stimulation [14].

Subsequently, the larger FIX-HF-5 study evaluated CCM in 428 patients with NYHA class III or IV symptoms and an LVEF ≤35% [15]. Although the trial did not meet its primary endpoint of anaerobic threshold, prespecified subgroup analyses identified significant clinical benefits in patients with moderately reduced LVEF (25% to 45%) [16]. To confirm these findings, the FIX-HF-5C trial was designed [17]. This prospective, randomized study randomized 160 patients with LVEF 25–45% and a narrow QRS to CCM plus GDMT versus GDMT alone [18]. The study met its primary efficacy endpoint, demonstrating a statistically significant improvement in peak $\text{VO}_2$ and quality of life, as well as a reduction in the composite rate of cardiovascular death and HF-related hospitalizations [19]. Furthermore, economic evaluations have demonstrated that CCM is a highly cost-effective intervention [20].

While initial devices utilized a three-lead system requiring an atrial sensing lead, the subsequent FIX-HF-5C2 trial demonstrated that a simplified two-lead Optimizer system (eliminating the atrial lead) achieved equivalent signal delivery, safety, and functional improvements [21]. This single-ventricular lead approach simplifies the implant procedure and reduces potential lead-related complications [22].

### Long-Term Outcomes, Safety, and Real-World Registries

Robust meta-analyses pooling data from randomized controlled trials have confirmed that CCM yields marked, consistent improvements in exercise capacity and quality of life [23, 24]. Although initial trials were not powered to detect differences in hard clinical endpoints, longer-term observational cohorts and registry data have addressed this gap [25].

An individual patient data analysis showed that CCM therapy is associated with a significant improvement in long-term survival compared to predictions from the Seattle Heart Failure Model [26]. Single-center and multicenter registries have corroborated these findings, demonstrating sustained reverse left ventricular remodeling (reductions in end-systolic and end-diastolic volumes) [27] and a significant reduction in hospitalization rates over follow-up periods exceeding two years [28]. Currently, CCM is approved by regulatory bodies and recognized in major consensus guidelines for symptomatic heart failure patients [29]. Ongoing clinical investigations are expanding the horizon of CCM, particularly for patients with heart failure and a higher ejection fraction [30]. In conclusion, CCM addresses a critical therapeutic gap for symptomatic heart failure patients ineligible for CRT. By enhancing calcium cycling and restoring healthy gene expression, CCM safely improves functional capacity, quality of life, and long-term outcomes.
